rows.description: When anger becomes threatening or violent, a person steps back, leaves the situation and seeks help, without trying to reason. Safety comes before conversation.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 7–12, 13–17

rows.subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
rows.description: A parent notices a child lying about homework or a broken item. Children mostly lie from fear of punishment, and a calm, safe way to admit truth reduces it.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26
related mind states: fear, calm, trust

rows.subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
rows.description: A parent senses secrecy about friends or online life. Privacy is developmentally normal, and worry should be matched with open questions and clear safety expectations, not interrogation.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 23–26

rows.subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
rows.description: A teenager conceals a failed year, a crush or trouble with a peer, expecting disapproval. Concealment feels safer short term but increases isolation and fear.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 23–26
related mind states: fear, shame, loneliness, trust

rows.subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
rows.description: A person who suspects a lie says I would rather know the truth than be protected, and that they will not explode. Lowering the cost of honesty makes it more likely, and accusations do the opposite.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17

rows.subtopic: Talking to someone lying or hiding
rows.description: A partner or family member finding repeated lies feels anger, self-doubt and grief. Boundaries and consequences protect trust, and talking with a counsellor or trusted friend helps regain clarity.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 7–12, 13–17
related mind states: grief, anger, doubt, trust

rows.description: A child interrupts because a thought feels urgent and might vanish. Giving a small signal, such as a hand on the arm, teaches waiting without silencing them.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A teenager talks over friends in energetic chat, meaning enthusiasm rather than rudeness. Some cultures and families treat overlap as warmth, and others feel it as disrespect.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: affection, admiration, excitement

rows.description: A student whose points are repeatedly cut off, or credited to someone else later, goes quiet. Repeated interruption may reflect gender, seniority or accent bias, and asking to finish the thought is legitimate.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A person who tends to talk a lot counts their own turns and asks others for input. Making space is a learnable habit and matters more the more senior or dominant one is.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 4–6, 13–17, 18–22
